Attack failed on every axis; this is the strongest of the four. WORDING: I pulled the raw wikitext of Page:Renascenceotherp00milluoft.pdf/28 (the scan-backed transcription of the 1917 Mitchell Kennerley edition) and it reads, character for character, 'The world stands out on either side / No wider than the heart is wide; / Above the world is stretched the sky,— / No higher than the soul is high.' The comma-plus-em-dash at the end of line 205 is the edition's own mark and is correctly reproduced; the em dash sits inside the quotation, where rule 5 does not reach (rule 5 bans the dash in the source and note only, and rule 7 requires the edition's punctuation). LOCATOR: this was the one claim worth breaking, and it holds. A WebFetch summary of the Wikisource transclusion page reported the poem as 264 lines, which would have put the quatrain elsewhere, so I did not trust it. I fetched all fourteen scan pages the poem transcludes (15 to 28) as raw wikitext, split on the explicit
marks, dropped the stanza-break blanks and the noinclude furniture, and counted: 12+16+16+16+16+15+15+15+16+15+16+16+16+14 = 214 lines. 'The world stands out on either side' is line 203 and 'No higher than the soul is high.' is line 206, with exactly eight lines following, so 'lines 203 to 206 of 214, in the closing twelve lines' is exact. The WebFetch line count was the small model miscounting. The foot of page 28 carries {{c|14}}, confirming printed p. 14. ATTRIBUTION: Millay's own signature poem, no misattribution-list entry touches it, no speaker to name (the poem's I is the poet's persona, not a named character). SHIPPED/CAP: shipped.js returns shipped [], near [], yearCount 0, atCap false, banned false. SCOPE: first printed in The Lyric Year 1912, collected 1917, so pre-1999; not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory; nothing needing a warning. FORM: source is 108 characters, leads with the author's name, has no dash, names work then locator then edition. Quotation ends in a full stop, no straight double quote anywhere, verse lineation preserved with ' / '. Tag Poetry is the form of the work. THEME: a rebirth poem for a month on Renewal, and the quatrain is expansive rather than bleak. One standing note for the editor, not a defect in this line: Millay, Teasdale and Kenyon are all United States, and April's carry-in pool already holds Kerouac, Twain, Emerson, Hemingway, Oliver and Brooks, so the 10-per-country cap is close to spent before the other lanes land.
